pages.text: Step inside a honey bee hive. Buzz, buzz! Many bees live here together as one busy family.
extras: A bee family is called a colony.

images.alt: A beehive frame full of honeycomb cells where honey bees live and store food

pages.text: Inside the hive, bees have different jobs. The queen is usually the mother of the hive. Worker bees do most of the hive work.
extras: Most hives have one adult queen.

images.alt: A marked queen honey bee surrounded by worker bees on the comb

pages.text: Some bees are drones. Drones are male honey bees. They have big eyes, but they do not collect nectar or pollen.

images.alt: A male drone honey bee flying through the air

pages.text: Worker bees build with wax from their own bodies. They warm the wax and shape it into tiny rooms called cells.
extras: Beeswax is a bee-made building material.

images.alt: A sheet of beeswax foundation stamped with a honeycomb pattern

pages.text: Look closely at the honeycomb. Many cells have six sides. Six-sided cells fit together neatly, side by side.
extras: A six-sided shape is a hexagon.

images.alt: A close view of golden honeycomb with many six-sided wax cells

pages.text: Out in the flowers, worker bees sip sweet nectar. A bee uses a long tongue to lap it up.
extras: Nectar is a sugary flower liquid.

images.alt: A honey bee sipping nectar from a flower with its long tongue

pages.text: Bees also carry pollen on their back legs. As they visit flowers, pollen can help flowers make seeds.
extras: Those leg pockets are pollen baskets.

images.alt: A honey bee on a flower with yellow pollen on its legs and body

pages.text: Back at the hive, workers pass nectar from bee to bee. They fan their wings until watery nectar becomes thick honey.

images.alt: Worker honey bees on golden honeycomb cells, with wings spread near uncapped honey cells

pages.text: When the honey is ready, bees seal the cell with a wax cap. Honey is food for times when flowers are hard to find.

images.alt: Worker honey bees crowded together on a sheet of honeycomb

pages.text: Honeycomb cells can hold baby bees too. Worker bees feed and care for the young bees as they grow.
extras: Baby bees grow from eggs to adults.

images.alt: Honeycomb cells opened to show bee eggs and young larvae

pages.text: A hive stays busy all day. Young workers clean and feed babies. Older workers guard, forage, and help move air through the hive.

images.alt: A single western honey bee standing on honeycomb

pages.text: When one bee finds good food, she can waggle dance. Her dance tells other bees where to fly. A hive is one big living team!

images.alt: A honey bee flying with pollen packed in the baskets on its back legs
